Patient Information: [redacted] Female, DOB [redacted], Hospital ID [redacted]. Admitted for chronic anicteric cholestasis and worsening cough with exertional dyspnea, diagnosed with chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) complicating sarcoidosis. Histopathological findings confirmed BCS with liver, gastric, and skin biopsies. Patient received oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation therapy and was discharged in stable condition.

Key Findings: The patient has diabetes mellitus evolving for 3 years without oral contraceptive use. Increased cholestatic enzymes (γ-glutamyl transferase 136 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase 325 UI/L) and normocytic inflammatory anemia with hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 82.8 fL, and serum ferritin 150 g/L were noted. Hepatomegaly with hypertrophied caudate lobe, splenomegaly, and portal hypertension were confirmed. Multinodular liver with absence of hepatic veins, centrolobular hepatocytes atrophy and fibrosis, and fibrosis were demonstrated. Mediastinal and hilar adenopathies with multiple micronodular opacities on lower pulmonary lobes were confirmed. Non-caseating granuloma on gastric biopsies and sarcoid granulomas on skin lesions were noted. ACE raised to 201 UECA, no tuberculin or bronchoalveolar lavage results.

Hospital Course: Patient started oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and warfarin anticoagulation. Additional tests were performed to screen for prothrombotic disorder but failed to identify an underlying condition. BCS was the most likely diagnosis. Patient responded well and was discharged in stable condition.

Follow-up: Scheduled appointments with primary care and specialist providers. Patient and family advised to continue medications, monitor symptoms, and report concerns.

The patient, a 57-year-old male with extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status 3, received a mechanical cardiac support (LVAD) due to severe heart failure following successful initial evaluation. Three months post-surgery, a chest X-ray showed mediastinal widening and lymphadenopathy. CT scans confirmed lymphadenopathy outside the chest. A mediastinoscopy revealed consistent SCLC pathology. The patient was removed from active cardiac transplantation. Chemotherapy with carboplatin and IV etoposide was initiated while hospitalized. After his first cycle, the patient decided not to continue chemotherapy and opted for hospice care. Complications included cellulitis, pseudomonal neutropenia, and protracted nausea. The treatment course was complicated by prolonged IV antibiotic therapy, renal issues, and pleural and peripheral edema. The patient was discharged home and passed away approximately 6 months post-chemotherapy.

Admitted for carcinoma of the right breast with enlarged axillary lymph nodes, diagnosed as postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma 20 months post radiation therapy. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy with anastrozole and abemaciclib was initiated as part of a clinical trial (NeoMONARCH). Adjuvant 3D conformal radiation therapy was delivered to the right breast and supraclavicular region.  

Radiation therapy resulted in moderate acute radiodermatitis with submammary moist epitheliolysis. Histology showed no malignant tumor, but dermal fibrosis and panniculitis were present with chronic perivascular inflammation.

Discharge instructions include scheduled checkups, monitoring affected areas, and sun protection.

A 29-year-old white male farmer was admitted with left upper-quadrant abdominal discomfort and unintentional weight loss. The patient was diagnosed with CML in chronic phase and initiated imatinib. After a 6-month course, pancytopenia occurred, leading to discontinuation of imatinib. She reported sand splash at the seaside and discontinued contact lens use ten days before admission. A biomicroscopic examination confirmed central keratitis and corneal scraping, with Acanthamoeba sp. cysts identified in the Giemsa-stained corneal scraping sample. The patient was treated with alternating topical fortified vancomycin, ceftazidime, propamidine isothionate 0.1%, and chlorhexidine at the clinic. Contact lenses and contact lens solution were not cultured. At the second visit, no growth was observed after inoculation of the corneal scraping specimen onto E. coli plates. The specimen was classified as a "T2" genotype "A. castellani" according to PCR and sequence analysis. The case was approved by the ethics committee at Uludag University Faculty of Medicine (2016-9/18), and informed consent was obtained from the patient.

Initial findings included hypopituitarism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, polyuria, and hypertonic hypernatremia, confirmed by MRI of the right-sided pituitary microadenoma. Long-term follow-up is recommended for patients with intrasellar germinomas to monitor for recurrence or progression.

The patient was diagnosed with purulent pericarditis and treated with intravenous ertapenem based on microbial cultures. A partial pericardiectomy and sepsis resolved. The source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear, but a CT scan and chest imaging confirmed no recurrence of pericardial effusion. The patient was discharged home on day 8 of hospitalization. Continued chemo-radiation therapy was initiated 2 months post-discharge. No recurrence of pericardial effusion was observed following a TTE 4 weeks post-discharge.

The patient's recovery was uneventful, and she was discharged with no restrictions, with a follow-up recommendation for further management.
